reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: A displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis through the growth plate, typically in overweight adolescents around the time of the pubertal growth spurt
Presents with hip, groin, thigh, or referred knee pain and a limp; knee or thigh pain in an adolescent must always prompt examination of the hip
A characteristic sign is obligatory external rotation of the hip when it is passively flexed, with limited internal rotation
Radiographs should include a frog-lateral view, as subtle slips are best seen laterally; a line along the superior femoral neck (Klein's line) normally intersects the epiphysis
Slips are classified by symptom duration (acute, chronic, acute-on-chronic) and by whether the child can weight-bear (stable versus unstable), which strongly influences the risk of avascular necrosis
It is an orthopaedic urgency: once suspected the child should stop weight-bearing and be referred promptly, as further slipping worsens the outlook
Treatment is surgical stabilisation, usually in-situ pinning to prevent progression, and the contralateral hip may be pinned if at high risk
Consider an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder (e.g. hypothyroidism, renal disease) in atypical, young, or bilateral cases
reference.pathophysiology: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs when shear forces exceed the strength of the proximal femoral physis, allowing the epiphysis to displace, typically posteriorly and inferiorly, relative to the femoral neck (so the neck effectively rotates anteriorly and externally on the head). The physis is mechanically weakest during the adolescent growth spurt, and obesity increases the mechanical load, while hormonal factors influence physeal strength, explaining associations with endocrine disorders. In unstable slips the epiphyseal blood supply, which runs along the femoral neck, is at high risk of disruption, predisposing to avascular necrosis. Residual deformity from a healed slip alters femoral head-neck morphology and can cause femoroacetabular impingement and early osteoarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Femoral neck stress fracture or trauma
Referred pain from other hip or spinal pathology
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and frog-lateral pelvic radiographs of both hips (the lateral view is key for subtle slips)
Assessment of Klein's line and the physeal appearance
MRI or ultrasound in equivocal cases or to assess a pre-slip
Endocrine and metabolic workup (e.g. thyroid function, renal function) in young, atypical, or bilateral presentations
Careful hip examination for loss of internal rotation and obligatory external rotation on flexion
redFlags: SURGICAL URGENCY: suspected SCFE requires immediate non-weight-bearing and prompt referral to prevent further slip
Unstable slip (inability to weight-bear) carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis
Adolescent knee or thigh pain that could be referred from an undiagnosed hip slip
Bilateral or very young presentation suggesting an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: Stable slips treated promptly with in-situ fixation generally do well, whereas unstable slips carry a substantial risk of avascular necrosis and chondrolysis; even after successful fixation, residual femoral head-neck deformity can cause impingement and predispose to premature osteoarthritis, so long-term follow-up is important.
pitfalls: Attributing knee or thigh pain to the knee and failing to image the hip, leading to missed or late diagnosis
Allowing continued weight-bearing on a suspected slip, risking further displacement and avascular necrosis
Missing a subtle slip by not obtaining a frog-lateral radiograph
Overlooking an underlying endocrine cause in atypical or bilateral cases
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Enforce immediate non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral once the diagnosis is suspected, to prevent further slippage
Perform in-situ fixation with a single cannulated screw as the standard surgical treatment for stable slips
Manage unstable slips with urgent gentle reduction and fixation, counselling on the high risk of avascular necrosis
Consider prophylactic fixation of the contralateral hip in young children or those with an underlying endocrinopathy
Investigate and treat an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder such as hypothyroidism or renal disease in atypical, young or bilateral presentations

Undertake surveillance for avascular necrosis, chondrolysis and residual femoroacetabular impingement, with corrective osteotomy or impingement surgery and long-term follow-up for premature osteoarthritis
